intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Kruer syndrome (KRRS) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the FBXO31 gene (609102) on chromosome 16q24.2.

checks.claim: Kruer syndrome (KRRS) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the FBXO31 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Collectively, this report confirms that a recurrent missense variant in FBXO31 causes a novel neurodevelopmental syndrome.
checks.explanation: The paper reports heterozygous de novo FBXO31 variants as causing the disorder. It does not use the name 'Kruer syndrome', but the draft's use of that name is standard nomenclature.

checks.claim: The FBXO31 gene is located on chromosome 16q24.2.
checks.evidence_quote: We also identified two unrelated cases with an identical DNM (encoding p.Asp334Asn; Fig. 2a and Supplementary Table 4) in FBXO31, which encodes the F-box only protein 31.
checks.explanation: The chromosomal location is not stated in the paper; it is standard gene nomenclature, which counts as supported under the task rules.

paragraphs.text: Kruer syndrome is an autosomal dominant neurodevelopmental disorder with prominent motor dysfunction. It is caused by a recurrent de novo missense mutation in FBXO31. Dzinovic et al. (2021) suggested that its emerging hallmarks were delayed psychomotor development, dysfunction of both the pyramidal and extrapyramidal systems (spasticity and dystonia), impaired expressive and receptive language, and intellectual disability. Galaz-Montoya et al. (2026) described a core phenotype of cerebral palsy, global developmental delay/intellectual disability, and speech impairment, with neuropsychiatric features and a subtle facial gestalt.

checks.claim: Kruer syndrome is an autosomal dominant neurodevelopmental disorder with prominent motor dysfunction.
checks.evidence_quote: Our data confirm a link between variant FBXO31 and an autosomal dominant neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by prominent motor dysfunction.

checks.claim: Kruer syndrome is caused by a recurrent de novo missense mutation in FBXO31.
checks.evidence_quote: We now identified a third individual with the recurrent FBXO31 de novo missense variant, featuring a spastic-dystonic phenotype.
checks.explanation: The paper describes the cause as a recurrent de novo missense variant.

checks.claim: Dzinovic et al. (2021) suggested that emerging hallmarks of the FBXO31-related disorder were delayed psychomotor development, pyramidal and extrapyramidal dysfunction (spasticity and dystonia), impaired expressive and receptive language, and intellectual disability.
checks.evidence_quote: Emerging hallmarks of FBXO31‐related disease seem to include a delay in psychomotor development, dysfunction of both pyramidal and extrapyramidal systems (as evidenced by the manifestation of spasticity and dystonia), impairments in expressive and receptive language, and ID.

checks.claim: Galaz-Montoya et al. (2026) described a core phenotype of Kruer syndrome comprising cerebral palsy, global developmental delay/intellectual disability, and speech impairment.
checks.evidence_quote: A core neurodevelopmental profile was observed and included cerebral palsy (mixed hypotonia, spasticity, and dystonia), global developmental delay/intellectual disability, and speech impairment.

checks.claim: Galaz-Montoya et al. (2026) described neuropsychiatric features and a subtle facial gestalt in Kruer syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: Neuropsychiatric features were sometimes prominent and included attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, anxiety, stereotypies, autistic features, and behavioral dysregulation.
checks.explanation: The abstract also states: 'A subtle but consistent facial gestalt was noted.'

paragraphs.text: Jin et al. (2020) described 2 unrelated patients (F218 and F699) from a cohort of 250 cerebral palsy trios. Both had spastic diplegic cerebral palsy, intellectual disability, expressive language disorder, and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Patient F218 also had gut malrotation, constipation, cleft palate, and strabismus, and brain MRI was normal. Patient F699 had strabismus and severe constipation, and MRI showed ventricular dilation with a thin corpus callosum.

paragraphs.text: Dzinovic et al. (2021) reported a 9-year-old Slovakian boy, the first child of unrelated healthy parents, who had a complex, non-progressive movement disorder dominated by spasticity and dystonia. In infancy he had hypotonia and delayed development. He spoke single words at 12 months but lost speech at 18 months. By age 2 years his hypotonia had converted to limb spasticity, worse in the legs, and he had dystonic posturing of all 4 limbs. A working diagnosis of spastic-dystonic cerebral palsy was made. At age 9 years he had generalized dystonia, spasticity, hyperreflexia, leg clonus, an unsteady spastic-dystonic gait, no expressive language, and moderate intellectual disability. He had no dysmorphic features. Brain MRI at age 3 years showed reduced parietal and occipital white matter volume and global white matter dysmyelination.

paragraphs.text: Galaz-Montoya et al. (2026) reevaluated 3 previously published individuals and described 4 additional probands with the recurrent de novo FBXO31 D334N mutation. The core phenotype comprised cerebral palsy (mixed hypotonia, spasticity, and dystonia), global developmental delay/intellectual disability, and speech impairment. Neuropsychiatric features were sometimes prominent and included ADHD, anxiety, stereotypies, autistic features, and behavioral dysregulation. The authors noted a subtle but consistent facial gestalt. Neuroimaging often showed a hypoplastic corpus callosum and posterior-predominant white matter changes, and 1 individual also had gray matter heterotopias.

paragraphs.text: Jin et al. (2020) performed whole-exome sequencing of 250 cerebral palsy parent-offspring trios. They found the same de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the FBXO31 gene, asp334-to-asn (D334N), in 2 unrelated patients. Sanger sequencing of the mothers, fathers, and probands confirmed that the mutation had arisen de novo. Asp334 is a conserved residue in the FBXO31 binding pocket and is thought to mediate hydrogen bonding to cyclin D1. Structural modeling predicted that the mutation changes the surface electrostatic charge around the cyclin D1-binding site. Fibroblasts from both patients had less cyclin D than control fibroblasts (P = 0.004).

paragraphs.text: In a Slovakian boy with spastic-dystonic cerebral palsy, Dzinovic et al. (2021) used trio whole-exome sequencing to identify a de novo heterozygous c.1000G-A transition in the FBXO31 gene, resulting in an asp334-to-asn (D334N) substitution. This was the same mutation previously reported in 2 unrelated patients with spastic diplegic cerebral palsy. The mutation was absent from gnomAD and from in-house exomes. It affects a conserved residue in the domain that interacts with the substrate cyclin D1, and it was classified as pathogenic. No other potentially disease-relevant variants were found.

paragraphs.text: Dzinovic et al. (2021) compared their patient with the 2 patients previously reported with the same mutation. All 3 had motor and/or speech delay, mild to moderate intellectual disability, neonatal hypotonia, and lower-limb-predominant spasticity, and each had been diagnosed with cerebral palsy. Only their patient had dystonia. Other features were each found in 1 or 2 of the 3 patients: congenital malformations (cleft palate and intestinal malrotation in 1), ADHD (2), strabismus or esotropia (2), and brain MRI abnormalities.

paragraphs.text: Jin et al. (2020) used whole-exome sequencing of 250 cerebral palsy trios to identify a de novo heterozygous asp334-to-asn (D334N) mutation in the FBXO31 gene in 2 unrelated patients with Kruer syndrome (KRRS). Both patients had spastic diplegic cerebral palsy, intellectual disability, expressive language disorder, and ADHD. Sanger sequencing of the parents and probands confirmed that the mutation had arisen de novo. Asp334 is a conserved residue in the FBXO31 binding pocket and is thought to mediate hydrogen bonding to cyclin D1. Structural modeling predicted that the mutation alters the surface electrostatic charge around the cyclin D1-binding site. Patient fibroblasts had less cyclin D than control fibroblasts (P = 0.004). The authors concluded that the mutation causes an apparent gain of function in cyclin D degradation.

paragraphs.text: In a 9-year-old Slovakian boy with KRRS, Dzinovic et al. (2021) used trio whole-exome sequencing to identify a de novo heterozygous c.1000G-A transition in the FBXO31 gene, resulting in an asp334-to-asn (D334N) substitution. The boy had spastic-dystonic cerebral palsy. The mutation was absent from gnomAD and from in-house exomes. It affects a conserved residue in the cyclin D1-interacting domain and was classified as pathogenic.

checks.evidence_quote: The analysis revealed that the proband was heterozygous for a FBXO31 c.1000G > A (p. Asp334Asn) missense substitution, which had occurred de novo.

paragraphs.text: Galaz-Montoya et al. (2026) reported 7 individuals with KRRS, 3 previously published and 4 newly described. All carried the recurrent de novo heterozygous c.1000G-A (D334N) mutation in the FBXO31 gene.
